lines.text: Every bakery wants its own website. So you rent a server, copy your shop onto it, put your logo on top, and send customers the address.
Then a customer types that address, gets one digit wrong, and orders tyres from a garage. So you buy a domain.
A DNS record that turns crumbwell dot shop into your server's address, for every visitor.
Now people type a name they remember, land on your menu, and it finally looks like a real shop.
Then two people order the last sourdough loaf at the same second, and your site happily confirms both. You only baked one.
It sold twice because every order lives in one text file, and two saves at once trample each other.
So you add a database. Every order is a transaction: check the stock, reserve the loaf, write the order, commit. All of it, or none of it.
Now the last loaf sells exactly once, and the second person sees sold out. But it all still lives on one disk.
At two a.m. that disk dies, and three months of orders die with it.
So you add backups: three copies, two kinds of storage, one in another city, and you test the restore. Now a dead disk is a bad morning, not a dead bakery.
Then a customer pays on café wifi, and the browser says not secure, because plain HTTP crosses the room as readable text.
So you add HTTPS. A certificate proves the site is yours, everything gets encrypted, and anyone listening hears noise.
Then a blogger in Sydney posts your cinnamon rolls, and every photo crawls across the planet from one small server. Eight seconds per page. That's latency.
So you add a CDN, copies of your images on servers close to every customer. Sydney now loads from Sydney.
Then Saturday morning hits, a TV show mentions you, two thousand people open the shop in the same minute, and your one server melts.
So you add a cache for pages that never change, and a load balancer that spreads visitors over three servers and skips any that's sick.
Then checkout fails for some people, and nobody can tell why. Was it the server, the database, the payment page?
So you add monitoring. An uptime check every minute, a log for every request, and an alert that wakes someone up.
Months later, Crumbwell is fast, backed up, secure, and fully watched.
Then a customer types crumbwell dot shop and gets: this site can't be reached. Because someone edited the DNS record on a Friday, typed one digit wrong, and went home.
